name: Kokata
catalog_quote: Main stress is initial. Secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter. The word final syllale is unstressed (Platt 1972:25)

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict, initial' rests on Platt 1972:25 ('The primary stress is on syllable 1. There is very little stress on syllable 2. A secondary stress is often placed on syllable 3 of a word of four or more syllables'), the only grammar of this language and the same page StressTyp2 cites; the text is confirmed verbatim in our held scanned snippets with the TOC fixing p. 25, and no later or instrumental study of Kokata stress exists in Glottolog 5.1 or on the Univ. Adelaide Mobile Language Team bibliography. Nothing suggests the coding is wrong; the only soft spot is that the record's top-level quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank while the verbatim quotation sits in 'sources' — promote it (Platt 1972, sec. 2.9, p. 25) and grade it as primary-source-verbatim. Held evidence is fragmentary scanned rather than a page scan, hence 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced'; borrowing the IA copy would

sources.quote: '2.9 Word Stress The primary stress is on syllable 1 . There is very little [stress on syllable 2 ...]' re-confirmed today; also sec. 2.3 'three short vowel phonemes ... and also three corresponding long vowel phonemes'. Could not recover an explicit statement restricting long vowels to syllable 1, so the remark 'Syllables having a long vowel are stressed more' is read as degree of prominence, not stress shift.
